messages.content: You coach a learner of Spanish (their own language is English) who is rewriting part of a real post before publishing it. Two people talk to them: a reader from the community, who speaks Spanish and reacts like a real person in the thread, and a tutor, who speaks English and addresses the learner informally, as a friendly tutor would. The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.

Where it will be posted: Email to a Spanish language school. Readers: The school's admissions contact, Sra. Morales.
The post so far:
<<<
Estimada Sra. Morales:

Mi nombre es Daniel y yo soy de Manchester, en Inglaterra. Le escribo porque quiero aplicar para el curso de septiembre. Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.

¿Es posible que usted me envía información sobre los precios? También tengo algunas preguntas. Primero, prefiero una habitación con familia / un piso compartido, no sé cuál es mejor para aprender. ¿Está el piso cerca de la escuela? Necesito una habitación tranquilo para estudiar. Segundo, ¿puedo traer mi bicicleta? Me gusta montar en bici y quiero explorar las montañas. Tercero, soy vegetariano (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat) y espero que la familia pueda cocinar algo para mí. Mi novia viene conmigo el primer fin de semana.

¿Me puede decir cuándo empiezan los cursos? Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes porque tengo que comprar el vuelo. Estoy seguro de que voy a pasar muy bien en su escuela. Mirando adelante a oír de usted.

Saludos,
Daniel Clarke
>>>
The spot: "Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos." in Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.
What is wrong there: The main reason is hard to find, because the opening sentence runs the girlfriend, the family meeting, the failure to understand and the eagerness to learn into one long run without a clear purpose.
What the writer means (confirmed by them): Everything this passage says now: every point, question, hedge and feeling in it stays; only how it is put changes.
The learner will now write this part themselves in Spanish. Prepare everything the session needs, in this order:
- reader: what the reader says on reaching this spot as it stands: one short line in Spanish (at most 15 words), in character (puzzled, curious, teasing; never a teacher). The reader cannot read English: an untranslated passage is simply a gap to them, so react to what is missing and never mention the other language.
- replaces: exactly "Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.", copied character for character (the text around it is someone else's business). ref must fit in its place.
- keep: every point, detail, question, hedge and feeling in replaces, as short English notes, in order. The reference must carry each one unless the writer's meaning above drops it.
- ref: the reference version: what a fluent member of this community would write here to say exactly what the writer means, in the writer's voice and register. Keep everything the writer already says that still serves this meaning (their evidence, their reasoning, their own words) and add only what is missing. Never invent facts the writer has not given, here or in what they told you: no scene, event, line or detail from a work, no names, numbers, dates, quotes or personal circumstances. Where the meaning needs one (the evidence, which scene, what happened to them), write a short placeholder in its place, in Spanish, between ⟨ and ⟩ (for example ⟨the scene you mean⟩), and the writer will fill it in. Where the problem is how the sentence is built (order, emphasis, angle, nominalisation), rebuild it the way this community would say it; do not stop at the smallest fix. Keep the strength the writer confirmed: where the problem is how something lands on its reader (too pushy, too blunt) and the writer means a firm need, a request or a demand, say it the way this place says such things politely and keep it firm; never turn it into something optional or a passing wish. Where the writer reached for an image or a joke, use this community's own equivalent if it has one rather than flattening it into plain words. Where the writer built a figure on purpose (a parallel or echo, a deliberate repetition, wordplay), ref keeps the figure and only puts natural words into it; the why note for such a word says the figure works and why the word changes. ref never says again what the post already says right before or after the replaced text (a reason or detail the next sentence gives stays there). ref replaces exactly the replaces text and carries every keep note and every name, title or label in it (a dish's name before its description, a person's name); it is the final text for that span: anything else wrong or unnatural inside it is fixed too, even where it is the writer's own wording. The writer's voice stays: casual spelling and capitalisation (all lowercase, capitals for emphasis, keysmashes, stretched letters, a missing apostrophe in a contraction), slang, emoji and the community's own shorthand, wherever fluent members of this community write that way too; so does a greeting or a word from another language used as flavour that readers will get. Names (characters, people, usernames, places, the community's terms) are the writer's: leave how they spell and capitalise them and which name they use, unless a reader could not tell who is meant. None of these is a problem in either pass. But wording carried over from English (a calque, a collocation, structure or set phrase a fluent writer would not produce) is not voice: it is a problem however casual the post. ref keeps that voice. Put [square brackets] around two to four single words that carry the key choices.
- alts: one or two other natural ways to say it, without brackets.
- pieces: three to eight hint pieces: the content words and short collocations (one to three words) that carry the meaning, including the writer's own words worth reusing. Each piece is Spanish words only: no grammar notes, glosses, symbols or instructions. A piece names a word, never how to use it ("worth", not "worth + -ing" or "worth coming"). Not consecutive chunks of ref, no function-word glue, no full clauses: the learner must still build the sentence. "x / y" offers a fork.
- construct: the one reusable pattern this spot teaches, as a learner would jot it in a notebook: at most eight words, a Spanish frame with one placeholder ("X left him + adjective", "What really got me was …"), optionally a short English gloss. Not a grammar formula.
- why: one entry per choice in ref that the learner might not make themselves. label: the Spanish words; note, in English: why this choice here, contrasted with what the learner wrote or would likely write, with a nuance or a tiny example when it helps. Concrete and specific, never "more natural" or "more appropriate" alone.
- checks: the mistakes this learner is likely to make on a first try, most important first: missing a part of the meaning, a structure carried over from English, the specific error already in their draft, a wrong word for this sense. For each: problem (what the grader should look for, in English); reader (optional: how the reader reacts when it happens, one Spanish line in character, only when the meaning really suffers); hint (English: a nudge that points at the gap without giving the words); tell (English: says the fix plainly, with the words).
- success: the reader's reaction once the learner gets it right: in Spanish, in character, at most 12 words, a reaction to what is now said (not a summary of it).
- prompt: the tutor's instruction in English to start writing: one short sentence that fits the size of the spot (a clause, a sentence, a passage). The writer has just confirmed what they mean, so do not restate it; never mention punctuation, span boundaries or what comes after; never contain any word or structure from ref.

Me he perdido.","replaces":"Vengo a mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.","keep":["Purpose: coming to improve my Spanish","Reason: my girlfriend is from Granada","Met her family last year","Failure, hedged: understood almost nothing","Strong eagerness to learn","Goal: to be able to talk with them"],"ref":"Vengo a mejorar mi español [por] mi novia, que es de Granada. El año pasado conocí a su familia, [pero] no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.","alts":["Quiero mejorar mi español por mi novia, que es de Granada. El año pasado conocí a su familia, pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.","Vengo a mejorar mi español por mi novia, que es de Granada. El año pasado conocí a su familia, pero no entendí casi nada, y tengo muchas ganas de aprender para poder hablar con ellos."],"pieces":["mejorar","novia","familia","entender","ganas","hablar"],"construct":"Vengo a mejorar mi español por X (I'm coming to improve my Spanish because of X)","why":[{"label":"por mi novia, que es de Granada","note":"Ties the reason to the purpose in one clause, instead of a colon that leaves the reader to work out the link. Without it, the sentence reads as a list of facts."},{"label":"El año pasado conocí a su familia, pero","note":"Splitting here gives the meeting its own sentence, so the 'pero' contrast lands clearly. Chaining everything with 'y' or ':' blurs the failure into the rest."}],"checks":[{"problem":"Negation dropped or flipped: 'no entendí casi nada' must keep 'no' so the meaning is that he understood almost nothing.","reader":"¿Entonces entendiste o no entendiste?","hint":"Check that the verb you use still carries a negative, since 'casi nada' only makes sense with it.","tell":"Keep 'no' before the verb: 'no entendí casi nada'."},{"problem":"The reason for coming is not linked to the girlfriend, so the sentence reads as two unrelated facts.","reader":"¿Y eso qué tiene que ver con tu español?","hint":"Use a single word after 'mejorar mi español' to say the reason is her.","tell":"Write 'por mi novia' right after 'mejorar mi español'."},{"problem":"Everything runs on in one sentence, with the girlfriend, the family meeting and the failure chained together.","reader":null,"hint":"Find a natural break after the fact about where she is from, and start a new sentence with the meeting.","tell":"End a sentence after 'de Granada' and start the next with 'El año pasado conocí a su familia'."},{"problem":"The goal loses the sense of 'being able to': 'para hablar' only says he wants to talk, not that he will be able to.","reader":null,"hint":"The verb 'poder' has to appear, since the point is ability.","tell":"Use 'para poder hablar con ellos'."},{"problem":"The eagerness is weakened, for example 'quiero aprender' without the strong 'muchas ganas'.","reader":null,"hint":"Keep the strong feeling with a phrase meaning 'I really want to'.","tell":"Use 'tengo muchas ganas de aprender'."}],"success":"¡Ah, por eso quieres hablar con su familia!","prompt":"Now write this part in Spanish, giving your reason first."}
